proposals.rationale: Recommended: immediate object/position contradiction resolves through a single understandable comparison; question must be followed by longitude scope.
proposals.text: How can a clock tell a ship where it is?
proposals.viewerPromise: Understand how a time comparison reveals longitude.

proposals.rationale: Concrete historical entry, but visually depicting H4 demands accurate reconstruction or licensed photography.
proposals.text: This watch helped ships find their longitude. How?
proposals.viewerPromise: Connect H4’s purpose with the actual navigation principle.

proposals.rationale: Accurate but less immediate; abstract somewhere else needs an early reference-meridian reveal.
proposals.text: At sea, knowing the time somewhere else could help reveal your longitude.
proposals.viewerPromise: Understand why the reference location matters.

proposals.rationale: Conceptually strong, but lacks the ship and physical object in the first moment.
proposals.text: How can a difference in time reveal a difference in position?
proposals.viewerPromise: Convert the time gap into an east–west angle.

proposals.rationale: Defensible error magnitude with corrected-time context; degree of longitude may be too abstract without a clear visual.
proposals.text: One minute of clock error can mean a quarter-degree error in longitude.
proposals.viewerPromise: Understand why keeping reference time accurate mattered.

proposals.rationale: History opening introduces Harrison before viewers know the question; avoid implying lunar observation mandatory.
proposals.text: Harrison’s watch helped answer an ocean navigation problem. But the watch needed the sky.
proposals.viewerPromise: Understand why timekeepers and celestial observation work together.
